item.title: [chicago.suntimes.com] Stinging from playoff exit, Cubs must make sure next year is different: ‘It’s time to look in the mirror’
item.dc:creator: Vinnie Duber
item.description: SAN DIEGO — Was it a successful season in Wrigleyville? It’s hard — even with baseball’s highest scoring lineup, best defense and best player — to judge 2026 as anything but a failure for the Cubs. They set championship-level expectations and World Series goals. Bowing out of the postseason after two games, their offense muzzled and MVP center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong a non-factor, before the calendar even flipped to October? They didn’t come close. “The goal is to win, and we didn’t play wel
item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO — Was it a successful season in Wrigleyville?
It’s hard — even with baseball’s highest scoring lineup, best defense and best player — to judge 2026 as anything but a failure for the Cubs.
They set championship-level expectations and World Series goals.
Bowing out of the postseason after two games, their offense muzzled and MVP center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong a non-factor, before the calendar even flipped to October?
They didn’t come close.
“The goal is to win, and we didn’t play well enough to do that,” third baseman Alex Bregman said. “It’s time to look in the mirror and get better.
“I know myself and a lot of these guys will be thinking about it every day of the offseason and let it fuel us. Just not good enough. We need to get better. In all areas.
“It starts now for everybody in this organization. Assess the year and come back and be better next year, because it wasn’t good enough.”
In the wake of such disappointment, there’s one overarching question: How does this not happen again?
It’s been back-to-back years of this, the Cubs dispatched by the rival Brewers in the NLDS a year ago. That was described as fuel for their fire this season, but the embers didn’t even burn long enough for a rematch.
Craig Counsell, whom the Cubs poached from those Brewers, has two early postseason exits in three seasons at the helm, with two years left on the contract that made him the game’s highest-paid skipper.
“We lost,” Counsell said. “There’s a response to it that we get to choose, and we’ve got to improve. Everybody can point at themselves and say, ‘We’ve got to get a little bit better.’
“We’re going to have to wait to accomplish the thing we really want to accomplish. … We didn’t finish it this year, and you hope that this has to be part of the journey to the ultimate prize.”
With the investments made in Counsell, Bregman, Crow-Armstrong and more, the expectations are not going to change. The Cubs will head into next season thinking World Series, just like this year.
But at least at the moment, they have a lot of questions to answer about how they’re going to get there.
What will make the 2027 group better equipped than the 2026 one?
That’s what the offseason — likely to be halted by a lengthy work stoppage — will teach us.
This was a roller-coaster campaign, with high highs and low lows, a lot of pitching injuries and a final-week downturn that came at exactly the wrong time.
The thoughts on the minds of everyone inside the losing clubhouse Wednesday were of further blows this team is about to take, the players who aren’t going to return, the pending free agents who were such a part of this group and its plan to deliver on those championship-level expectations.
“We’ll talk about the baseball plenty,” second baseman Nico Hoerner said, “but when you get through a locker room with people that you’re really close with and people that aren’t guaranteed to come back here — and not seeing this thing through the way a lot of us envisioned and believed in — that’s the stuff that doesn’t sit right and hurts.”
Perhaps most important for Jed Hoyer’s front office, the Cubs might have to replace their entire starting rotation, with lefties Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga and David Peterson, plus righties Clay Holmes and Kevin Gausman, all set to hit free agency.
Righties Cade Horton, Edward Cabrera and Ben Brown, plus lefty Justin Steele, make for an intriguing group of possible replacements, but all are coming off injuries, a risky play.
Then there’s the corner outfielders.
Right fielder Seiya Suzuki has been an offensive force it will be tough for the Cubs to replace; he’s expected to be one of the best hitters on the market and land a big contract.
Left fielder Ian Happ is a franchise fixture whose potential departure had teammates crying Wednesday night.
“He embodies the Cubs more than anyone I know,” shortstop Dansby Swanson said through tears.
Sentimentality is a rare reason to spend for baseball front offices. Happ didn’t have the type of offensive season he consistently has throughout his career though still played excellent defense and hit for power.
“All I can say is that I love being a Cub,” Happ said. “I’ve loved my time. I’ve loved the place, the people, Wrigley Field, the fan base. And it’s been truly special. I don’t think there’s a better place in baseball to play.”
With decisions to make, how Hoyer crafts his roster – and how these Cubs respond to another bout of playoff disappointment – will answer that overarching question, the only question that matters:
How do the Cubs make sure this doesn’t happen again?

item.title: [MLB.com] What's it like to face Miz? We asked those who have
item.dc:creator: Adam McCalvy; Zach Sweet

The Cubs had faced Jacob Misiorowski more than most teams. Their manager still described a fastball at the top of the strike zone that “nobody can hit.” The Phillies came within one Kyle Schwarber swing of literally g
item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE -- To the Twins, it looked like a fastball you could see out of the hand – and then it was past you. To the Rockies, it was a pitch that seemed to reach the plate before they could react. The Braves geared up for 100 mph, then found themselves chasing cutters and sliders.
The Cubs had faced Jacob Misiorowski more than most teams. Their manager still described a fastball at the top of the strike zone that “nobody can hit.” The Phillies came within one Kyle Schwarber swing of literally getting no hits in nine innings.
“You see some guys that throw 103 [mph], but you get a little bit more time. A guy like that, where he's almost dropping it in the catcher's mitt, man, it makes for a tough day,” Judge said in May, after Misiorowski struck out 11 and touched 103.6 mph in his first career start against the Yankees. “I was excited to get a chance to face him and see him for the first time.
“You know, I’ve seen a lot of his games and seen what he's done; it's impressive stuff, man. They've got a great, great, great young star over there.”
Across the league, opponents spent the season looking for an answer when Misiorowski was on the mound. They struggled, as he finished with a 1.80 ERA, 252 strikeouts, a 0.80 WHIP and a .157 opponents’ average, each the best mark in the Majors. He enters October as the clear favorite for the National League Cy Young Award. On Saturday, the Padres will get the next chance when Misiorowski starts Game 1 of the National League Division Series.
Ask the hitters who faced him what makes the assignment so difficult, and velocity is only the beginning.
“Marshy asked me after the game,” said Phillies star Bryce Harper in June, referring to teammate Brandon Marsh, “he's like, ‘That's probably the best guy I've ever faced.’ And he asked me who’s one of the best guys I've ever faced, and I said Matt Harvey. He had that extension heater, and he was one of the first guys that really rode that heater at the top of the zone. Obviously, 104 [mph] is a little bit different.”
That was after Misiorowski’s finest start of the season, a 15-strikeout, 27-batter, 95-pitch shutout in front of a spellbound crowd at American Family Field on June 12, the one-year anniversary of Misiorowski’s Major League debut.
Harper, perhaps with October in mind, saw a silver lining.
“I'm happy we were able to face him – and I'm not saying that in a good way or bad way, but I was just happy we were able to face him and see what that looked like,” he said.
The Twins had their own trouble in an Aug. 9 matchup, when Misiorowski reached 200 strikeouts faster than all but one pitcher in history. Misiorowski began that night by throwing 21 consecutive four-seam fastballs. Royce Lewis saw one at 103 mph in his first at-bat and called it one of the most difficult pitches he had ever faced.
Brooks Lee noticed how far Misiorowski’s 6-foot-7 frame carried him down the mound, and how his position on the first-base side of the rubber changed the angle. Even a hitter who recognized what was coming had little time to do anything about it.
“It comes out of his hand and you feel like you see it well, and then it’s by you,” Twins hitter Kody Clemens said. “Especially up in the zone.
“If he throws a fastball in the upper part of the zone, I feel like it’s damn near impossible to hit.”
Twins manager Derek Shelton pointed to the pitch’s movement near the top of the zone. Hitters had to judge whether it would be a ball or strike while trying to catch up to 100-plus mph. He called it “probably one of the most challenging at-bats in the game.”
“Honestly, we were scratching, clawing, trying to get to him in any way, shape or form,” Colorado outfielder Cole Carrigg said.
Misiorowski threw 66 pitches at 100 mph or harder that day, a single-game record in the pitch-tracking era. Rockies manager Warren Schaeffer saw more than a radar-gun reading.
“That’s a one-of-one fastball, 103 with all that extension,” Schaeffer said. “It’s hard to react to that. And he throws it all the time.”
Against Atlanta in August, the problem changed shape. Misiorowski threw six scoreless innings in a matchup with Chris Sale, a pitcher he grew up admiring. Sale left impressed by “probably the most impressive fastball I’ve ever seen.” Braves manager Walt Weiss explained what happened when hitters prepared for it.
“You’re gearing up for 100, and then you’re having to deal with cutters and sliders,” Weiss said. “It’s among the toughest at-bats.”
The Cubs’ Seiya Suzuki had offered a similar assessment after facing Misiorowski in June, on the night he fired a 105.5 mph fastball against Pete Crow-Armstrong to match the third-fastest pitch since tracking began in 2008.
“Everybody had good swings and good at-bats,” Suzuki said through interpreter Edwin Stanberry, “but overall, he just pitched better.”
The Cubs did find a way through on Sept. 2 at Wrigley Field, scoring five runs in the first two innings and chasing Misiorowski after four while snapping his streak of 25 consecutive outings allowing three or fewer earned runs. Alex Bregman homered on a slider low in the zone and added a two-run single on a 102 mph fastball. Beforehand, Cubs manager Craig Counsell had identified the opening: Get a pitch lower in the zone, because the high fastball was so hard to hit even when hitters expected it.
“When he executes, you’re in trouble,” Counsell said. “That’s generally how the great ones are.”
Six days later, the Cubs saw him again. Misiorowski opened by striking out Crow-Armstrong on a 103.7 mph fastball, reached 104.5 against Suzuki and allowed one run over 6 1/3 innings. Along the way, he threw his 1,000th pitch of the season at 100 mph or harder.
“That’s how I throw,” Misiorowski said afterward. “The guys on the other side expect that.”
They do. By now, hitters from New York to Philadelphia to Minnesota to Colorado to Atlanta to Chicago, and across the entire league, can describe the fastball, the angle and the pitches that follow.
The Padres will arrive with their own plan. Then someone will have to stand in the box and try to make it work. Nobody has consistently done that against the presumptive NL Cy Young winner in 2026.

item.title: [reviewingthebrew.com] 3 reasons Brewers fans should be encouraged by NLDS matchup with Padres, 2 reasons to be nervous
item.dc:creator: Owen Jonas
item.description: After sweeping the Chicago Cubs in the NL Wild Card Series, the San Diego Padres have officially punched their ticket to the NLDS, where a matchup with the top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers awaits them. It will be the Brewers and Padres' first-ever meeting in the postseason, and there are no two hotter teams in baseball right now. The Brewers and Padres each posted a 18-6 record during the regular season portion of their September schedule, and San Diego added two more convincing wins over the Cubs t
item.content:encoded:
After sweeping the Chicago Cubs in the NL Wild Card Series, the San Diego Padres have officially punched their ticket to the NLDS, where a matchup with the top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers awaits them. It will be the Brewers and Padres' first-ever meeting in the postseason, and there are no two hotter teams in baseball right now. The Brewers and Padres each posted a 18-6 record during the regular season portion of their September schedule, and San Diego added two more convincing wins over the Cubs this week.
While Brewers fans are relieved not to have to deal with the added stress that comes with facing the Cubs in the postseason, the Padres' recent performance undoubtedly has some fans wishing for a matchup with Craig Counsell's squad. That said, for as well as the Padres are playing right now, there are still certainly reasons for Brewers fans to be encouraged by the specific matchup. Let's take a closer look at three of the Padres' weaknesses and how they might come into play in the NLDS.
3 reasons Brewers fans should be encouraged by their NLDS matchup with the Padres
1. Question marks remain in San Diego's starting rotation
Heading into the postseason, the Padres' rotation was certainly their biggest weakness. With an elite bullpen and a surging offense, fans were unsure what San Diego would get from their starting staff in October. However, the duo of Michael King and Nick Pivetta, the latter of whom had a limited regular season workload this year due to an early-season elbow injury, dominated the Cubs in the Wild Card series, allowing just one earned run in a combined 10.1 innings. King's seven-inning shutout on Tuesday night did the heavy lifting, but Pivetta certainly impressed on Wednesday night as well.
However, even if King and Pivetta replicate their Wild Card performances in the NLDS -- likely in Games 2 and 3 -- questions remain in regard to the rest of San Diego's starting options. Trade deadline acquisitions Casey Mize, who is currently hurt, and Robbie Ray, who snuck onto the Wild Card roster but didn't pitch, haven't panned out as the Padres hoped they would. Long-time Los Angeles Dodger Walker Buehler also made the Padres' initial playoff roster, and is certainly a candidate to start a game, but his pedestrian 4.63 ERA in 32 starts this year doesn't necessarily scream "postseason starter." Not only will San Diego need King and Pivetta to repeat their incredible Wild Card performances in the NLDS, but they will also need another less obvious postseason starter to step up.
2. Padres' league-average infield defense bodes well for Brewers' offensive approach
The Cubs had an elite defensive unit in 2026, that much was obvious. In addition to Pete Crow-Armstrong's impressive performance in center field, the Cubs' infield of Alex Bregman (who was limited to DH in the Wild Card series due to a freak injury), Dansby Swanson, Nico Hoerner, and Michael Busch took away a number of would-be base hits thanks to their impressive range and sure-handedness. The Padres, while their infield unit is fine, by no means have the same elite ability to take away ground-ball base hits, and is therefore a better matchup for the Brewers' offense.
Manny Machado remains a strong defender when it comes to Outs Above Average (OAA), but his Defensive Runs Saved (DRS) total tells a different story. Ty France is a solid defensive first baseman, but the duo of Xander Bogaerts and Jake Cronenworth up the middle is below-average in the field. It's an important part of this series because the Brewers rank first in MLB in Batting Average on Balls in Play (BABIP), third in infield hits, and second in bunt hits. In other words, Milwaukee puts a lot of pressure on opposing infield defenses, and the Padres' shaky unit could come back to hurt them in this series.
3. San Diego's offense was far closer to league average for a majority of the season
The Padres' offense is on fire right now. No team posted a higher collective batting average, slugging percentage, or wRC+ than the Padres during the month of September, and only the Brewers scored more runs. Strong final months from Fernando Tatis Jr., Jackson Merrill, France, and Bogaerts led the Padres to these impressive numbers during the month of September, but for a majority of the season, San Diego's offense looked far closer to league average.
From the start of the season to the end of August, San Diego held a collective wRC+ of 98, indicating that their offensive unit was below league average for the first five months of the season. During that stretch, they ranked 20th in home runs and 22nd in runs scored. Their strong final push made their season-long numbers appear far better, but for a majority of the 2026 season, San Diego's offense was not among the best in baseball. That could matter not if the Padres' recent hot streak continues throughout October, but it's important to note this recent performance is the exception, not the norm.
2 reasons Brewers fans should be nervous about their NLDS matchup with the Padres
1. The Padres are the hottest team in baseball (aside from maybe the Brewers)
Whether their recent performance is the exception or not, there's no denying that the Padres are one of the two hottest teams in baseball, with their only threat being the team they will match up against in the NLDS. As previously mentioned, the Brewers and Padres finished first and second, respectively, in runs scored during the final month of the regular season en route to MLB-best 18-6 records. The Padres then stymied a strong Cubs' team with two comfortable wins in the NL Wild Card Series.
For the Brewers, who seemingly run into the hottest team in baseball in the early rounds of the postseason every single year, a matchup with the Padres feels like more bad luck. San Diego surged to the top Wild Card spot in the NL, secured a home postseason series, swept said series, and now carries that momentum into the NLDS. That certainly doesn't feel like a fair draw for the best team in baseball, who just completed a record-breaking 103-win regular season. Yes, the Padres have more flaws on their roster than the Brewers, but sometimes all that matters is how a team is playing when the postseason rolls around, to which the recent performance of each of these two teams would suggest fans are in for a competitive series.
2. San Diego is the only team with a better bullpen than the Brewers
The Brewers are heading into the postseason with their bullpen at its best, which is not often the case following the 162-game season. The combination of Trevor Megill, Abner Uribe, and Aaron Ashby at the back end, trade deadline acquisitions JoJo Romero and Antonio Senzatela in the middle innings, and multi-inning options like DL Hall, Chad Patrick, and Shane Drohan has Milwaukee's relief corps among the best in baseball as the playoffs arrive.
However, if there's one bullpen group that is better than the Brewers', it's the Padres' ridiculous assembly of relief weapons. Flame-throwing closer Mason Miller and his elite set-up man Adrian Morejon rightfully garner much of the attention, but other arms like Bradgley Rodriguez, Jason Adam, who just returned from the 60-day IL, and southpaw Yuki Matsui deserve respect as well. Given the strength of San Diego's bullpen and the question marks in their rotation, the pressure will be on the Brewers to build early leads and take advantage of as many scoring opportunities as possible.

item.title: [MLB.com] Lights-out bullpen deployed to perfection in Padres' Wild Card Series clinch
item.dc:creator: Cole Bradley
item.description: SAN DIEGO -- The lights cut out, Korn’s “Blind” blared, the sellout Petco Park crowd rose to their feet roaring and Mason Miller seemingly spawned onto the mound for the start of the ninth inning. The game was over. The National League Wild Card Series was over. But in reality, it had ended well before that. This is exactly why Padres general manager A.J. item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO -- The lights cut out, Korn’s “Blind” blared, the sellout Petco Park crowd rose to their feet roaring and Mason Miller seemingly spawned onto the mound for the start of the ninth inning. The game was over. The National League Wild Card Series was over.
But in reality, it had ended well before that.
This is exactly why Padres general manager A.J. Preller assembled the best and deepest bullpen in baseball, for nights like Wednesday.
“In the postseason, you’ve got to get a lot of great hitters out,” Preller said. “You’ve got to have a lot of answers in that bullpen.”
After starter Nick Pivetta departed in the fourth, Padres manager Craig Stammen fully unleashed his bullpen over the final 5 2/3 innings against the Cubs in Game 2. Bradgley Rodriguez, Jason Adam, Adrian Morejon and Miller proceeded to allow just three men to reach base and keep Chicago’s league-best offense scoreless to slam the door on a 4-1 victory and send the Padres to the NL Division Series for a best-of-five-series against the Brewers.
Michael King going seven scoreless innings in Game 1 and saving the key arms in the back end set the Padres up perfectly to lean on that group the following night. If the Padres got an early lead, Stammen wasn’t going to mess around with keeping Pivetta in longer than he needed to secure the series.
That’s exactly how things played out.
San Diego scored a pair of runs in the second before Pivetta -- who did his job in limiting the Cubs over 3 1/3 innings -- got the hook in the fourth after giving up an RBI single to Nico Hoerner. A one-run lead ballooned to three after Gavin Sheets’ pinch-hit homer in the bottom half of the inning. The ‘pen took care of the rest.
“Michael’s effort last night was phenomenal and that allows us to go out firing in the early part of the game today and get our best guys out there,” Miller said. “It puts us in a really confident position. We get a lead and we feel really good about it.”
Perhaps the most important aspect of the Padres’ performance in this series was shutting down the Cubs’ elite lineup, and specifically their top two hitters in Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman. The former is coming off the seventh 40-40 season in baseball history and the latter posted a 1.010 OPS in the second half.
They collectively went 0-for-15 in the series with eight strikeouts.
It was quite the statement, but it’s exactly what the Padres have been doing all season. By innings, San Diego had the fourth-most used bullpen in the Majors (683 2/3) and it possessed the fifth-best ERA (3.53).
“It’s an incredible group, top to bottom,” Adam said. “It doesn’t matter the situation, it doesn’t matter the inning, everybody out there is ready to go at all times. Fourth inning, ninth inning, I don’t care who we put out there, I feel really confident the guy is getting the job done.”
Rodriguez was the first into the fray, the rookie right-hander who immediately became one of the best relief arms in the sport and has been dominant in high-leverage situations throughout the year. He played fireman in the fourth, escaping a bases-loaded jam to preserve Pivetta’s line before pitching a clean fifth that he capped with a strikeout of Seiya Suzuki on a changeup below the zone.
“We’ve always known that about Bradgley -- that his maturity level is beyond his years,” Padres pitching coach Ruben Niebla said. “He doesn’t rattle. He doesn’t get nervous. He trusts himself and is a confident guy. We’re able to put him in those situations very confidently, and he’s responded well to that.”
Adam got through a 1-2-3 sixth, then Morejon cruised through the seventh and eighth, allowing just one hit, a Tyrone Taylor single. Then the ball was handed to Miller, the most imposing reliever in the game, who struck out an insane 47.4% of the batters he faced this season and finished with a career-best 1.67 ERA and 38 saves.
He gave up a double to Hoerner but struck out a pair and got Carson Kelly to ground out to end it, sending the Padres to Milwaukee and the Cubs back home.
“It’s not about any individual, it’s about a group,” Miller said. “It’s about passing the ball to the next guy and getting us in the clubhouse with a win. I think it’s a lot of selfless guys down there.”
Now, the Padres get the top-seeded Brewers in the NLDS, another team with plenty of firepower in the bullpen. To defeat them, and anyone else standing in the Padres’ way this October, Wednesday will be the template.
And if it continues to pan out the way it did, that should scare the rest of the postseason field.
“We knew we had six innings we could cover,” Niebla said. “It worked out to perfection.”

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] MLB Playoff Roundup: Alec Bohm’s 10th-inning homer forces Game 3 against Braves
item.dc:creator: Peter Brody
item.description: What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa. The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the post
item.content:encoded:
What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa.
The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the postseason on Wednesday so let’s jump straight into the action!
AL Wild Card Series Game 2
Chicago White Sox 7, Houston Astros 3
(Chicago wins 2-0)
After just two games, I can’t think of any playoff participant who wants to face these White Sox. That is a sentence that no one could conceive of typing at the start of the season. Two seasons removed from suffering the most losses in MLB history and on the back of three straight losing campaigns, this upstart Chicago squad came out of nowhere to crash the postseason, starting with a two game sweep of the Astros in their own building.
They have done so by scoring early and often, the White Sox lineup a deep unit one-thru-nine with multiple ways to hurt you. They work deep counts, foul pitches off, draw walks, and can put the ball in play, but can also slug the ball out of the yard from almost any spot in the batting order. On Tuesday, they scored three unanswered runs in the first two innings to put the Astros on the back foot from the word go, and Wednesday continued the trend with the Southsiders hanging a four-spot before the home team had a chance to bat.
They had a 1-0 lead just five pitches into the game against Astros ace Hunter Brown, Sam Antonacci leading off with a double before Kyle Teel drove him home with a single. A fielding error by Nick Allen on a Miguel Vargas grounder put a pair on, and three straight singles by Andrew Benintendi, Tristan Peters, and Chase Meidroth plated three more runs with help from a Lucas Spence throwing error from center.
Credit to the Astros, they did not roll over after going down four in the first and slowly chipped into the White Sox lead. Jeremy Peña led off the bottom of the first with a booming home run that clattered off the left field wall just below the train tracks. Cam Smith hit one to almost exactly the same spot with two outs in the second. Jose Altuve narrowly snuck a solo shot into the Crawford Boxes to lead off the fourth and just like that, a 4-0 game had become a 4-3 thriller.
An inning later it looked like the Astros would pull of the improbable and complete the comeback. Smith was hit by a pitch, Peña singled, and Isaac Paredes walked to load the bases with two outs for Altuve. However, reliever Anthony Kay got Altuve to fly out to medium right field to strand all three ducks on the pond. That left the door open for the White Sox to swing the momentum back in their own favor and they did so immediately. Benintendi and Peters drew a pair of walks to open the sixth, prompting Joe Espada to call on Bryan Abreu out of the bullpen. Astros owner Jim Crane vetoed a trade of Abreu to the Twins in the final minutes of the deadline, and Abreu rewarded that faith by hanging a 3-1 slider to Meidroth, the second baseman crushing a three-run bomb to left to put the final nail in the Astros’ coffin.
After sweeping this rematch of the 2005 World Series, the White Sox advance to the ALDS where they will face the AL Central champion Guardians, first pitch of Game 1 scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET on Saturday.
NL Wild Card Series Game 2
Philadelphia Phillies 4, Atlanta Braves 3
(Series tied 1-1)
The Phillies’ season was hanging by a thread until some late heroics by Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper, and Alec Bohm sent this thrilling series to a decisive Game 3. It was a pitchers’ duel early between two starters trending in opposite directions. Tyler Mahle entered his first career playoff start with a sub-two ERA after joining the Braves from the Giants at the deadline while Cristopher Sánchez posted an ERA above five in the month of September (though will still likely wrap up his second straight runner-up finish in NL Cy Young balloting).
The one thing the two starters do have in common is first inning struggles and that certainly played out in this game. Mahle allowed a leadoff double to Trea Turner and consecutive one-out singles by Bryce Harper and Alex Bohm to allow the Phillies to jump ahead, 1-0. However, Sánchez issued a leadoff walk to Ronald Acuña Jr., who promptly stole second and scored the tying run on a Matt Olson single.
Both starters settled in from there, trading zeroes for the next five innings, until things unraveled for Sánchez and his defense in the seventh. Sean Murphy worked a leadoff walk and Ha-Seong Kim reached on a bunt single to put a pair on with no outs. Drake Baldwin then clubbed what looked like a routine liner to right, but Harper misplayed it horrifically breaking in on the ball only to watch it sail over his glove and to the wall for what was ruled as an RBI double. Sánchez intentionally walked Ozzie Albies to load the bases, and Olson made him pay with a sac fly to double the Braves lead, 3-1.
What should have been a hammer blow to the Phillies morale did not play out as such. Schwarber immediately responded with a towering leadoff shot off lefty reliever Dylan Lee, and Harper atoned for his misplay by going back-to-back to retie the game, 3-3. That sent this game to extra innings, where the much-maligned Alec Bohm continued his redemption tour. Bohm was on the bubble of being non-tendered during the offseason, but the Phillies kept him around and drove in the first run of the series with an RBI double in the first inning of Game 1. The third baseman was the ultimate hero in this one, his opposite field solo homer off rookie Didier Fuentes in the 10th to keep the Phillies season alive and force a decisive Game 3.
San Diego Padres 4, Chicago Cubs 1
(San Diego wins 2-0)
This game featured surprisingly quick hooks of both starters as neither manager wanted to risk leaving their highest leverage relievers unused. One was certainly more deserved than the other, Kevin Gausman allowing three runs on five hits in 3.1 innings. The Cubs were desperate for starting pitching at the Trade Deadline and Gausman was supposed to be their big prize. However, he flopped after making the move from the Blue Jays, pitching to a 4.83 ERA in nine starts post-deadline, and his stinker tonight was the beginning of the end of the Cubs’ season. Nick Pivetta on the other hand held Chicago to a run on three hits and two walks with four strikeouts in 3.1 innings, but Craig Stammen seemed determined to play the matchups in this one.
Ty France got things started with a double to lead off the second, advancing to third on a Jackson Merrill single, who then stole second to put a pair in scoring position for Xander Bogaerts. The veteran shortstop opened the scoring with an RBI single, which brought Ethan Salas to the plate. The 20-year-old became the youngest catcher ever to appear in a playoff game, and in his first postseason PA, he lifted a sac fly to center to plate Merrill as the Padres’ second run.
The real story of this series has been the Cubs’ inability to score. They led MLB scoring 5.25 runs per game, spearheaded by shoo-in NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong and his MLB-leading 45 home runs (PCA would go 0-for-7 with four strikeouts in the series). They found themselves shut out through the first 12.1 innings of this series, finally breaking the seal in the fourth on a Seiya Suzuki single, Ian Happ walk, and Nico Hoerner RBI single. A Carson Kelly hit-by-pitch loaded the bases with two outs, but Dansby Swanson flew out to stand all three in place.
San Diego immediately punished them for failing to fully cash in on that scoring opportunity. Bogaerts reached on a one-out double, prompting Craig Counsell to call on Daniel Palencia in relief of Gausman. Palencia yanked a 101 mph fastball right into Sheets’ nitro zone down and in, and the lefty crushed it to right for a mammoth two-run blast.
It was all hands on deck from there from the Padres bullpen looking to protect their lead for the final five innings of the contest. They proved how terrifying a relief corps they’ve been all season, allowing just three base runners — a Michael Busch walk with two outs in the fifth, a Tyrone Taylor pinch-hit single with one out in the eighth, and a Hoerner one-out double off Mason Miller in the ninth — after the Cubs stranded the bases loaded to end the fourth.
San Diego advances to the NLDS where they will face the best team in baseball. It’s an unenviable position to come up against presumptive NL Cy Young Jacob Misiorowski and the 103-win Brewers. Game 1 of that series is scheduled for October 3rd with first pitch time contingent upon the result of Game 3 between Philly and Atlanta.

item.description: One of two National League Wild Card Series wrapped up on Wednesday night when the San Diego Padres completed their two-game sweep of the Chicago Cubs. The series win for San Diego means it will hit the road and travel to the Midwest for an NLDS showdown against the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers. item.content:encoded:
One of two National League Wild Card Series wrapped up on Wednesday night when the San Diego Padres completed their two-game sweep of the Chicago Cubs.
The series win for San Diego means it will hit the road and travel to the Midwest for an NLDS showdown against the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers.
The two teams met six times in the regular season, with the Padres taking four of six games from the Brewers. Let's dive into who performed well from each side in those six games.
Offensively for San Diego, it was a bit of an unlikely hero in the regular season series. First baseman Ty France was outstanding against the Brewers, slashing .389/.421/.556, good for an OPS of .977 with a homer and three walks.
Wednesday's playoff hero Gavin Sheets also was stellar against Milwaukee, slashing .308/.471/.589, good for an OPS of 1.009 with four walks and a game-winning home run early in the season.
The San Diego bullpen arms were also solid, especially Adrian Morejon and Mason Miller, who combined for five shutout innings across five appearances.
Ty France drills a solo home run to left field and cuts the Padres' deficit to 2-1 in the bottom of the 2nd!
Brewers @ Padres#MLB #ForTheFaithful pic.twitter.com/fzfv1Pd9GQ
GAVIN SHEETS 9th-INNING HEROICS
Down to their last out, the @Padres have rallied! pic.twitter.com/yO0CxqvN33
Milwaukee did not have much offensive success against San Diego, averaging just 3.5 runs per game. There were still encouraging signs, though, especially from the first base duo of Jake Bauers and Andrew Vaughn.
Bauers had 18 at-bats against the Padres, slashing .278/.381/.444 with three doubles and three RBI. Vaughn hit .294 with two RBI in 17 at-bats.
NL CY Young frontrunner and Game 1 starter Jacob Misiorowski made one start against the Padres in the regular season and it was excellent. Misiorowski tossed seven shutout innings with zero walks and 10 strikeouts. Left-hander Kyle Harrison was also good against the Padres, posting a 2.79 ERA across two starts and 9 2/3 innings.
10 strikeouts for Jacob Misiorowski
He completes 7 IP for the first time in 2026! pic.twitter.com/nsJoZX3DVp
Milwaukee has a slight advantage in the starting pitching department, but the two bullpens may be the deciding factor in the series.
They ranked first and third in the National League in ERA this season and the ultimate deciding factor may be which bullpen blinks first and lets a late lead slip away.

item.content:encoded:
October baseball is upon us, and we have a massive playoff game on Thursday night.
The Philadelphia Phillies and Atlanta Braves are the only teams remaining in the wild card round, setting up a standalone Game 3 on Thursday night.
The Phillies came back from a 3-1 deficit in Game 2 – after a key Bryce Harper error – to win in extra innings behind solo shots from Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Alec Bohm.
The starting pitching matchup for Game 3 is murky at the moment, although two beat reporters gave some insight into what these teams might do.
Long-time Phillies reporter Jim Salisbury shared that he’s hearing veteran Aaron Nola will get the start for the Phillies while the Braves will go with an opener in Ray Kerr. The Atlanta bullpen is elite, ranking fourth in MLB in ERA during the regular season.
Braves beat reporter Mark Bowman also shared some insight to the starting pitching matchup, mentioning that Braves righty Grant Holmes could be used as the “bulk” option behind Kerr on Thursday. He also believes the Phillies will use a combo of Nola and ace Zack Wheeler, who would be pitching on short rest after leading the Phillies to a win on Sunday.
All hands are going to be on deck in this matchup for both teams, as this is a win-or-go-home scenario.
Oddsmakers have set the Phillies as slight favorites on the road, a sign that they have more confidence in Philly’s options to start in this game.
Here’s a breakdown of the odds, a player prop to bet and my prediction for Thursday’s Game 3.

- Braves +1.5 (-174)

Phillies vs. Braves Best MLB Prop bets
Braves Best MLB Prop Bet
- Drake Baldwin OVER 1.5 Hits, Runs, RBIs (-108)
In today’s edition of Walk-Off Wagers – our MLB Best Bets column at SI – I shared why Baldwin is worth a look if Nola gets the start:
If Nola ends up getting the start, it’s a good sign for Braves catcher/designated hitter Drake Baldwin.
Baldwin picked up two hits and a run batted in on Wednesday, and he’s fared extremely well against Nola in his career.
The 25-year-old is 5-for-11 (.455) against Nola in his career, with a .955 OPS. He’s driven in one run against the Phillies veteran, and Nola has struggled quite a bit with the long ball this season, allowing 37 in 33 starts during the regular season.
A homer would immediately hit this prop for Baldwin, and he’s coming off a strong showing on Wednesday. During the regular season, the Braves star hit .284 overall and .307 against right-handed pitching.
Baldwin also entered the playoffs on a hot streak, batting .360 with two home runs, five runs batted in and a .951 OPS over the final two weeks (12 games). He’s a pretty interesting bet with this prop set at -108 on Thursday.
Phillies vs. Braves Prediction and Pick
Another play from today’s Walk-Off Wagers, I’m going to back the Phillies to win and advance after stealing Game 2:
There’s certainly an argument to be made for the Braves, who went 23 games over .500 at home in the regular season, but I lean with the Phillies in Game 3.
If Wheeler is able to pitch on short rest in any capacity, he’ll be by far the best pitcher in this game and had a massive finish to the regular season. Wheeler had a 1.71 ERA in September, lowering his season-long ERA to 3.00. He may not be able to give the Phils a ton of length, but it should help ease the pressure on their bullpen.
Nola has pitched in a ton of big games in his career, and I don’t want to downplay his two solid starts against Atlanta earlier this month. In two outings, Nola allowed just 10 hits and three earned runs across 13.1 innings of work.
The Braves have only used Kerr as an opener once this season, and Holmes had some very shaky advanced numbers in the regular season, ranking in the 12th percentile in expected ERA and the 18th percentile in expected BAA.
The Atlanta bullpen has been taxed in this series, pitching Didier Fuentes, Dylan Lee and Rasiel Iglesias in back-to-back days. That’s not nothing. Can the Atlanta ‘pen hold up after blowing Game 2?
I’d much rather take the Phillies and their proven veteran starters in a winner-take-all game, especially after they showed they can power themselves to a win on Wednesday.
Pick: Phillies Moneyline (-118 at DraftKings)

item.description: Whenever a baseball team wins a postseason series and celebrates with champagne and drinks in the locker room, it seems like reporters are just as much a part of the party as the players. item.content:encoded:
Whenever a baseball team wins a postseason series and celebrates with champagne and drinks in the locker room, it seems like reporters are just as much a part of the party as the players. And who wouldn’t want to celebrate with John Fanta?
The San Diego Padres were the last team to celebrate late Wednesday night, sweeping the Chicago Cubs in two games to win their Wild Card series. And much like we saw in Chicago with the White Sox and in New York with the Yankees, there were festive scenes. And while nobody quite did it like Muretaka Murakami with the South Siders, the Padres at least had NBC’s energetic and affable reporter/host/announcer in their clubhouse.
Fanta interviewed Padres superstar Fernando Tatis Jr. in the locker room and asked about how the team found their groove after a mediocre first 100 games of the season. He also asked Tatis to look ahead to the challenge of facing the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLDS and ace pitcher Jacob Misiorowski.
But honestly, all we wanted to see was John Fanta get doused with some kind of alcoholic beverage. And that’s what Tatis delivered. A bottle of Bud Light was the shower of choice. Thankfully, Fanta was wearing a clear plastic parka because he knew what was coming, too.
A conversation and a Bud Light shower with Fernando Tatis Jr.
The San Diego Padres are rolling on to Milwaukee. pic.twitter.com/LVyKbvxvIS
— John Fanta (@John_Fanta) October 1, 2026
We have certainly come a long way since the days when Tim McCarver and Deion Sanders shared a tense moment with the Atlanta Braves all those years ago, when he got his own bath in the locker room.

item.content:encoded:
MLB playoff schedule 2026: Full bracket, scores, times, TV channels to watch every postseason series originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
More than seven months after pitchers and catchers reported to spring training, it's time to determine which team will wear the MLB crown in 2026.
Twelve teams reached the postseason bracket, and any discussion about favorites has to start with the two-time defending champion Dodgers. Los Angeles wasn't necessarily dominant during the regular season and enters October with concerns about the health of the planet's best player, Shohei Ohtani, but it has proven unwise to bet against LA lately.
While the Dodgers are in the midst of a dynastic run, neither of the teams that owned the best records in their respective leagues during the regular season — the Brewers and Rays — has won a World Series. Victory would be particularly sweet for either of those fan bases, along with the other postseason entrant without a title, the Padres.
Who will survive the gauntlet to lift the Commissioner's Trophy at the end of October? Here's when and where to watch every game.
Where to watch MLB playoffs 2026
- TV channels: Fox, FS1, TBS, NBC, NBCSN
The 2026 MLB postseason will have a new look for the opening round, with NBC carrying every wild card game on its platforms: NBC, NBCSN and/or Peacock.
After that, the familiar rotation returns. This year's NL playoffs will air on Fox or FS1 while the AL will be on TBS, with the World Series set to air on Fox as it has every year since 2000.
Fans can stream every postseason game except Peacock exclusives with DIRECTV, which offers a free trial to new subscribers.
All games airing on NBC, NBCSN, Fox and FS1 can be streamed with fubo, which also offers a free trial.

item.description: The postgame celebrations in the San Diego Padres’ locker room after beating the Chicago Cubs in the NL Wild Card game were absolutely lit. So lit, in fact, that team owner Kwanza Jones was cutting it up with the rest of the team. Video shared on social media by reporter Marty Caswell shows San Diego Padres star Fernando Tatis Jr. dancing with Kwanza Jones during the team’s locker room celebration after the Padres swept the Chicago Cubs in the Wild Card Series on Wednesday night. Padres owner Kw
item.content:encoded:
The postgame celebrations in the San Diego Padres’ locker room after beating the Chicago Cubs in the NL Wild Card game were absolutely lit. So lit, in fact, that team owner Kwanza Jones was cutting it up with the rest of the team.
Video shared on social media by reporter Marty Caswell shows San Diego Padres star Fernando Tatis Jr. dancing with Kwanza Jones during the team’s locker room celebration after the Padres swept the Chicago Cubs in the Wild Card Series on Wednesday night.
Padres owner Kwanza Jones joined Fernando Tatis Jr. in popping bottles and dancing in the clubhouse after San Diego swept the Cubs
I never completed this interview with Kwanza Jones, thanks to @tatis_jr
@@FriarTerritory pic.twitter.com/kxmqAmsH3o
— Marty Caswell (@MartyCaswell) October 1, 2026
Why yes, Fernando Tatís danced with Kwanza Jones pic.twitter.com/E993DYRC78
— Marty Caswell (@MartyCaswell) October 1, 2026
Tatis finished the Wild Card Series against the Cubs 2-for-7 with one home run, one RBI, three runs scored, one walk and one stolen base.
Jones and her husband, José E. Feliciano, were unanimously approved by MLB owners on Aug. 17 in a $3.9 billion deal, the richest franchise sale in league history. Jones is MLB’s first Black woman majority owner, while Feliciano serves as the team’s control person under league rules.
When the Padres clinched a playoff spot at Dodger Stadium on September 24, Tatis danced on the infield grass and hugged Jones, while a video of Feliciano chugging a beer bong with pitcher Walker Buehler went viral on social media.
The Padres closed out the Cubs with a 4-1 win in Game 2 at Petco Park, finishing a sweep after surging through September as one of baseball’s hottest teams. The NLDS against Milwaukee starts Saturday night.
With their win over the Cubs in the NL Wild Card Round, the Padres have advanced to the National League Divisional Series, where they’ll take on the Brewers. The series will kick off in Milwaukee with Game 1 on Saturday, October 3.

item.dc:creator: Redacción OnCuba
item.description: La segunda jornada de la Serie de Comodín en la temporada de las Grandes Ligas (MLB, por sus siglas en inglés) selló el adiós de los dos cubanos más mediáticos de la Liga Americana: el slugger Yordan Álvarez y el lanzador Aroldis Chapman. Los Astros de Houston, de los que Yordan fue bujía a lo largo de la campaña, cayeron en apenas dos juegos ante los Medias Blancas de Chicago, mientras a los Medias Rojas de Chapman los frenaron en seco uno de los exequipos del cerrador holguinero: los Yankees e
item.content:encoded:
La segunda jornada de la Serie de Comodín en la temporada de las Grandes Ligas (MLB, por sus siglas en inglés) selló el adiós de los dos cubanos más mediáticos de la Liga Americana: el slugger Yordan Álvarez y el lanzador Aroldis Chapman.
Los Astros de Houston, de los que Yordan fue bujía a lo largo de la campaña, cayeron en apenas dos juegos ante los Medias Blancas de Chicago, mientras a los Medias Rojas de Chapman los frenaron en seco uno de los exequipos del cerrador holguinero: los Yankees en Nueva York.
Los Medias Blancas ganaron este miércoles 7-3 en Houston y completaron la barrida sobre los Astros. Así, dejaron sin opciones al tunero de seguir ensanchando la mejor campaña de su trayectoria, coronada con el liderazgo de bateo del circuito con promedio de .316, además de despachar 42 jonrones y luchar por la Triple Corona hasta el final del calendario regular.
Houston, we don’t have a problem pic.twitter.com/NmPM6SCndJ
— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) October 1, 2026
Poco pudo aportar Yordan a la causa, al irse en blanco en cuatro visitas al plato. Con ello dejó su producción ofensiva en la postemporada en solo un imparable en los ocho turnos oficiales sumados por él en los dos choques disputados.
La suerte estuvo siempre del lado visitante, pues Chicago anotó cuatro veces en el primer episodio ante el abridor Hunter Brown, ayudado por errores defensivos. En lo adelante, los Astros solo pudieron responder con jonrones solitarios de José Altuve, Jeremy Peña y Cam Smith.
Este duelo era el de mayores expectativas entre los aficionados cubanos dada la presencia en el bando de Chicago del joven antesalista Miguel Vargas, quien tuvo su mejor temporada en la fase preliminar, pero no ha tenido un feliz estreno en la instancia decisiva.
El habanero volvió a fallar en cinco turnos, lo que, unido a un similar desempeño en el choque anterior, lo mantiene a la espera de su primer imparable en la postemporada.
Esta vez el protagonismo recayó en Chase Meidroth, autor de un vuelacercas de tres carreras, y en el bullpen encabezado por Erick Fedde y Jordan Hicks, quienes no permitieron hits en cuatro entradas combinadas para apuntalar la victoria de Anthony Kay.
3-RUN POSTSEASON HOMER FOR CHASE MEIDROTH! pic.twitter.com/39yNEWjiLt
— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) September 30, 2026
Boston desarmado
En el Yankee Stadium, los dueños de casa complacieron a sus parciales con la segunda victoria seguida ante los Medias Rojas de Boston, esta por 9-2. El éxito dejó sin opciones de supervivencia a sus archienemigos históricos y marcó el cierre de temporada para su cerrador estrella Aroldis Chapman.
Max Fried trabajó seis entradas, con seis ponches y una carrera limpia, y fue respaldado por Cody Bellinger al conectar jonrón y producir cuatro anotaciones.
CODY BELLINGER THREE-RUN HOMER
IT’S 8-1 YANKEES! pic.twitter.com/gUQC8CJQb9
— MLB (@MLB) October 1, 2026
Luis García Jr. también firmó un significativo aporte al batear de 5-3 con otro vuelacercas, signo de la oportunidad de los bateadores del Bronx, quienes ligaron de 9-6 con corredores en posición de anotar.
Sonny Gray cargó con la derrota, que tampoco pudieron evitar varios relevistas, entre ellos Garrett Crochet y Garrett Whitlock.
Chapman, sin oportunidad de cerrar un juego ajustado en la serie de comodín, tuvo una entrada de actuación en la que ponchó a los tres bateadores que enfrentó.
Con ese despliegue se convirtió en el primer jugador nacido en Cuba con participación en 10 postemporadas de MLB, y en el segundo de Latinoamérica con 10 o más experiencias de este tipo, solo superado por el legendario panameño Mariano Rivera (16).
¡EL MISIL SIGUE HACIENDO HISTORIA! 🇨🇺
Aroldis Chapman se convierte en el 2do jugador nacido en Latinoamérica en participar en 10 diferentes #Postseason uniéndose a Mariano Rivera. pic.twitter.com/1VjtJcLAZO
— MLB Español (@mlbespanol) October 1, 2026
Además, con los tres ponches recetados llegó a 76 ponches en octubre, para colocarse en el listado histórico de relevistas por detrás de Rivera (110) y Kenley Jansen (94).
Con 38 años, el holguinero cerró una de sus mejores experiencias de las últimas temporadas. A lo largo del tramo regular fijó una efectividad de 1.92 carreras limpias por juego, con 35 salvamentos y 71 ponches en 51.2 entradas.
Sin Cachorros en juego
Las cosas también fueron bien en casa para los Padres de San Diego, al despachar por segunda ocasión sucesiva a los Cachorros de Chicago, esta vez con pizarra de 4-1.
Gavin Sheets conectó jonrón de dos carreras, al tiempo que Xander Bogaerts y Ty France aportaban dos hits cada uno.
Summer’s over, we’re on to October. pic.twitter.com/I4KRWqSyyf
— San Diego Padres (@Padres) October 1, 2026
La ocasión fue propicia para que el relevista cubano Adrián Morejón debutara en la serie lanzando dos entradas en blanco, con un hit permitido, sirviendo de puente hacia los cerrojos de Mason Miller y Jason Adam.
Todo lo contrario sucedió en Atlanta, donde los Filis de Filadelfia lograron equilibrar el pulso con una victoria 4-3 sellada en 10 entradas, que extendió hasta este jueves la definición del trámite.
Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper y Alec Bohm combinaron su poder con jonrones para la causa de los visitantes, mientras que el joven Andrew Painter retiraba a los bateadores de Atlanta durante tres entradas en blanco para quedarse con la victoria.
Well, that was wild pic.twitter.com/FpU4KdGxXo
— Philadelphia Phillies (@Phillies) September 30, 2026
El relevista cubano Raisel Iglesias trabajó un inning por los Bravos, con un hit permitido y sin tolerar carreras.
A la espera de esta decisión, los Medias Blancas se alistan para enfrentar a los Guardianes de Cleveland en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana, que arranca el venidero sábado 3 de octubre.
Por su parte, los Yankees enfrentarán con el mismo objetivo a los Rays de Tampa Bay, que cuentan en su filas con los cubanos con el cubano Yandy Díaz y Victor Mesa Jr.
En la Liga Nacional, San Diego pactó su choque con los Cerveceros de Milwaukee —el mejor equipo de la temporada regular con 103 victorias— y los actuales campeones, los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, con el cubano Andy Pagés entre sus referentes, aguardan para conocer su primer rival en la ruta hacia la conquista de su tercera Serie Mundial consecutiva.

item.title: [MLB.com] Padres get revenge with commanding sweep of Cubs in Wild Card Series
item.dc:creator: AJ Cassavell
item.description: SAN DIEGO -- The Padres spent September as the hottest team in baseball, surging into the postseason and securing a Wild Card Series at Petco Park. item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO -- The Padres spent September as the hottest team in baseball, surging into the postseason and securing a Wild Card Series at Petco Park.
All summer, Sheets had been playing through a nasty injury -- a plantar plate tear in his left foot. He wondered if he’d be able to contribute at all. There was certainly no way he could contribute defensively.
But maybe … just maybe … if Sheets could heal just enough … he could deliver a meaningful swing or two in the postseason.
A swing like this one.
Sheets came off the bench to deliver the swing that broke the Cubs in Game 2 of the National League Wild Card Series on Wednesday night -- a pinch-hit, two-run home run that sent Petco Park into delirium and the Padres on course for Milwaukee.
With their 4-1 victory over the Cubs, San Diego secured a trip to the NL Division Series against the Brewers, beginning on Saturday night. But first, the Padres staged a party in the home clubhouse at Petco Park.
Before the champagne was popped and the cigars were lit, manager Craig Stammen stood at the center of it all.
“We had 13 bricks to lay,” Stammen said. “Two down, 11 more to go.”
The next three almost certainly won’t come quite so easily. For the fourth time in seven seasons, the Padres are headed to the NLDS, where they’ll meet Milwaukee in a playoff series for the first time. The Brewers own the sport’s best record. Jacob Misiorowski, the presumptive NL Cy Young Award winner, takes the ball first.
“We know who they’re throwing Game 1,” said Xander Bogaerts. “So let’s celebrate today. And then be ready for that fastball.”
Call it sweet revenge for the Padres after their 2025 season came to an end with a Wild Card Series exit at Wrigley Field.
They made quick work of the Cubs, dispatching them in two games that were never all that close. The two teams played 18 innings at Petco Park this week. The Padres led after 17 of them. The Chicago offense, which scored more runs than any other team during the regular season, was held to one across two playoff games.
“We just didn't play well enough,” said Cubs manager Craig Counsell. “And they're playing really well.”
In Game 1, the Padres were a force of nature. The ballpark partied from the very first pitch (a Michael King fastball past Pete Crow-Armstrong) to the very last pitch (Joe Musgrove punctuating his triumphant return to the mound with a game-ending strikeout). They won, 8-0.
“I’ve never seen anything like it,” Manny Machado, a veteran of eight postseasons, said of the home crowd this week. “That was huge.”
Game 2 brought a different kind of postseason energy. A party, to be sure. But one with some tension mixed in. October baseball, on the final day of September.
San Diego jumped in front in the second with Bogaerts’ RBI single and Ethan Salas’ sacrifice fly. (Salas, the youngest player in history to catch a postseason game, also became the youngest player at any position with a postseason sac fly -- since at least 1954 when that stat was fully tracked.)
But the Cubs scratched a run back against Nick Pivetta in the fourth and worked their way into the Padres’ bullpen. Crow-Armstrong and the top of the lineup loomed in the fifth.
There were two outs and a runner aboard, and Counsell had gone with right-hander Daniel Palencia. Sheets strode to the on-deck circle, then, eventually, the batter’s box -- with those three familiar thuds echoing through the Petco Park sound system.
HO-LY SHEETS.
“You just get ready for that moment, so when it happens you don’t feel like it’s sped up on you,” Sheets said. “To see this fanbase the whole entire time, I just wanted to get in front of them, I wanted to play. These guys brought it.”
This was the moment the Padres had been planning for. When Sheets is right, he mashes right-handed pitching. He’s a weapon in the clutch and can be a force off the bench.
“We had talked about that move, probably more than I care to admit in my office, with our pro scouting and advanced scouting,” Stammen said. “We felt like Gavin was a good matchup for some of their right-handed pitching. … That’s why we put him on the bench today, just in case he could pop one like that in a big situation.
“Doesn’t always work out that way. But he made us all look good.”
In the end, Sheets would take all of one swing across two games in the series. He made it count.
Palencia threw a 100.8 mph fastball at the bottom of the zone on the inner half. Sheets turned on it -- the hardest pitch any Padre has ever homered on, regular or postseason.
“That’s Dairy Bonds, baby,” said Jackson Merrill, between puffs of a cigar in a raucous Padres clubhouse. “That’s what he does -- 101, down and in. You just don’t see that. That was sick. That was one of the cooler home runs I’ve ever seen.”
And then get ready for that fastball.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- Just when it looked like Willson Contreras had given the Red Sox some much-needed life with a solo homer to right-center with two outs in the sixth inning of Game 2 of the American League Wild Card Series against the Yankees, the season essentially went up in flames in a disaster-filled bottom of the frame.
The Statcast-projected 387-foot shot felt significant in the moment because it snapped a drought for the Red Sox of 26 postseason innings without a run dating back to Game 2 of last year’s Wild Card Series (also against the Yankees).
But the Bronx Bombers made the short burst of momentum from Contreras feel insignificant when they erupted for six runs in a game-breaking, series-breaking bottom of the sixth inning that sent deafening roars throughout Yankee Stadium and the Red Sox to a 9-2 loss on Wednesday. Those reverberating sounds were a harsh reminder to the Red Sox that this was likely to be their last game of 2026.
With two flat performances in the final two nights of September, during which they were outscored, 18-2, the Red Sox were denied a chance to play in October. It also extended the streak to five straight seasons of no postseason baseball at Fenway Park.
“Regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there were quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series, and that ended for us tonight,” said Red Sox manager Chad Tracy. “So it's frustrating. And there's a lot of things you can say, but in the moment, right now, I think the guys only care that we lost. And it's going to take some time to get over that.”
It will go down as a roller-coaster spring, summer and brief autumn in Boston. There was the 32-46 hole, which the Sox somehow dug out of with a season-altering 32-5 stretch from June 25-Aug. 7 that included a franchise-tying winning streak of 15 games.
Then there was the final month of the regular season, which included injuries to key players and a stunning lack of offense, two themes that carried into the postseason.
“I'm proud of what we accomplished,” said veteran starter Sonny Gray, who took the loss. “Sour taste in your mouth for the ending. But we were left for dead there for a while, and I will definitely remember that run that we went on and what that felt like, because I've never experienced anything like that in my career -- to dig ourselves out of that hole and to put ourselves in this situation, that was a lot of fun.”
For the Red Sox, the fun ended in New York before it even started.
Quite simply, very little went right for the Sox in this two-game sweep at the hands of their rivals, which lacked the drama of last year’s set that went the distance (also won by the Yankees).
“For our season to end the same way that it did last year against our biggest rival, it sucks” said Red Sox lefty Garrett Crochet.
The bottom of the sixth served as a microcosm of the futility and frustration -- the inning that deep-sixed Tracy and his club.
With Contreras creating some energy in the Boston dugout, Tracy tried to add to it by bringing on Crochet for his first appearance in a game since April 25.
Crochet’s quest to get back in time for postseason play after left shoulder woes was a compelling storyline for the Red Sox, but one that didn’t work in real time.
The lefty seemed to get off to a solid start when he struck out Spencer Jones on a sweeper. But catcher Adley Rutschman’s block wasn’t a clean one, and he appeared to hesitate before throwing to first after retrieving the wild pitch. The initial call of out was overturned on replay. Jones then stole second and moved to third on Rutschman’s throwing error.
From there, things devolved. Crochet didn’t get an out and was charged with four runs, though only one of the three hits he allowed was well-struck.
“Personally, to think that I busted my [butt] the past five months, and for it to end that way, on a personal note, it's tough,” said Crochet. “I just wanted to come back and contribute to the team as best I could, and I let them down.”
Gray turned in a strong enough start for the Sox, giving up six hits over 4 2/3 innings and leaving with his team down 1-0.
But the offense never quite came around, and the bullpen had a second straight spotty night. And just like that, the season was over.
“Obviously disappointed,” said shortstop Trevor Story. “A lot of thoughts. Proud of this group, proud of this team. With all the [criticism] and everything around, the way this team came together, and really turned the season around to get back into this position is something that was special, and we're not going to forget that. Obviously, it's not about doing amazing things in the regular season. It’s about the postseason.”

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Will Joey Ortiz Be Ready for the Brewers' NLDS Opener on October 3?
item.dc:creator: Miracle Dimwesh
item.description: Pat Murphy provided an update on Joey Ortiz as the Milwaukee Brewers prepare for their National League Division Series opener. item.content:encoded:
Pat Murphy provided an update on Joey Ortiz as the Milwaukee Brewers prepare for their National League Division Series opener.
Ortiz underwent an MRI over the weekend, with Murphy saying the structural results were good. However, the Brewers manager remains cautious because Ortiz is dealing with a bruised right knee and abdominal swelling.
Ortiz has not played since leaving Milwaukee's Sept. 25 game against the St. Louis Cardinals in the eighth inning.
Brewers Manager Pat Murphy said Andrew Vaughn is a full go this week, but they are still keeping an eye on Joey Ortiz’s abdomen and knee.
Murphy says Ortiz will be a “little limited” and they are keeping him from some of the higher intensity activities in today’s workout.
The Brewers have extra time to monitor Ortiz because their 103-59 regular season earned them a first-round bye. Milwaukee will open the NLDS on Oct. 3 against the winner of the Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres Wild Card Series.
Ortiz was an important part of the Brewers' infield during the regular season. He appeared in 134 games and hit .270 with a .328 on-base percentage, .402 slugging percentage, nine home runs, 47 RBI and nine stolen bases.
Ortiz also recorded 100 hits, 14 doubles and four triples while drawing 35 walks. His availability could give Milwaukee another option in the infield as the team begins its postseason run.
For now, Murphy is giving Ortiz time rather than rushing him back into game action. The seven-day window between his last regular-season appearance and the NLDS gives the Brewers additional time to evaluate his condition.
Milwaukee enters October after winning 103 games, but Ortiz's health is one of the situations the team will continue monitoring before Game 1. His status should become clearer as the Brewers get closer to their postseason opener.

item.title: [yardbarker.com] Blue Jays planning to re-explore Japanese market this offseason
item.dc:creator: Vanessa Serrao
item.description: According to Toronto Blue Jays president and CEO Mark Shapiro, the team plans to re-explore the Japanese market this offseason. The Blue Jays will also be sending a contingency plan to Japan in the offseason, and Shapiro plans to travel there as they look to bolster the lineup. On Sept. 8, he became the fifth Japanese-born player to hit 30 home
item.content:encoded:
According to Toronto Blue Jays president and CEO Mark Shapiro, the team plans to re-explore the Japanese market this offseason. The Blue Jays will also be sending a contingency plan to Japan in the offseason, and Shapiro plans to travel there as they look to bolster the lineup.
The Blue Jays have already been successful with recruiting Japanese star Kazuma Okamoto, who had a stellar rookie campaign this season with 33 home runs. On Sept. 8, he became the fifth Japanese-born player to hit 30 home runs, earning a noteworthy milestone achievement.
Signing Okamoto to a four-year, $60 million contract last offseason was a massive win. While the team's offense and power output took a significant step backward this season, Okamoto was the driving force behind the team's power. All things considered, his success has persuaded the team to continue to find more Japanese talent.
While the Blue Jays are targeting Seiya Suzuki from the Chicago Cubs as well, the team has also been eyeing two big Nippon Professional Baseball (NPB) stars who are expected to be on the market this winter and have already gained significant attention from MLB teams.
Mark Shapiro says the #BlueJays will send a contingency to Japan this offseason and he may travel there, too, as they look to expand their presence (both baseball and business).
He added that the Japanese market will obviously be something they explore again this winter.
Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato and right-handed pitcher Kaima Taira are two talents that would help enhance the Blue Jays' needs ahead of the 2027 season. Sato would provide the Blue Jays with an elite left-handed power bat who is coming off a dominant 37-home-run season with an explosive 1.012 OPS for the Hanshin Tigers.
With Taira, he is expected to be one of the top arms on the market alongside Tarik Skubal, who is an elite starter and reliever. But as a starter, he led all of NPB with a 1.36 ERA, serving as a commanding presence for the Saitama Seibu Lions.
The Blue Jays would benefit from adding his arm, as he would provide high-upside pitching depth to the rotation as well as a bullpen safety net. His versatility makes him an intriguing option to add as the team faced a heavily taxed pitching staff this season. While the Blue Jays are expected to get Cody Ponce, Bowden Francis and Jose Berrios back in 2027, you can never have enough pitching, and this past season proves it.

item.title: [heavy.com] Los Angeles Dodgers Announce 3 Sudden Roster Moves Amid MLB Playoffs
item.dc:creator: TJ French
item.description: The MLB playoffs are in full swing, as Wild Card matchups began this week. For the Los Angeles Dodgers, they are still awaiting their opponent for the NLDS. It will be either the Atlanta Braves or the Philadelphia Phillies. Amid the MLB playoffs, the Dodgers made a few roster moves in preparation for their upcoming series. More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Announce Tyler Mahle News After Dramatic Phillies Game Los Angeles Dodgers Make 3 Roster Changes The Dodgers do know that they will begin the
item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are in full swing, as Wild Card matchups began this week.
For the Los Angeles Dodgers, they are still awaiting their opponent for the NLDS. It will be either the Atlanta Braves or the Philadelphia Phillies.
Amid the MLB playoffs, the Dodgers made a few roster moves in preparation for their upcoming series.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Announce Tyler Mahle News After Dramatic Phillies Game
Los Angeles Dodgers Make 3 Roster Changes
The Dodgers do know that they will begin their quest for a three-peat on Saturday, October 3.
In the meantime, here are the three roster moves the team made, per the team’s transactions tracker:
“Los Angeles Dodgers activated RHP Edgardo Henriquez from the 15-day injured list.”
“Los Angeles Dodgers recalled LHP Ronan Kopp from Oklahoma City Comets.”
“Los Angeles Dodgers recalled SS Hyeseong Kim from Oklahoma City Comets.”
The most notable roster move of the trio is Edgardo Henriquez being activated from the 15-day IL, which could be a huge boost to the Dodgers’ bullpen. However, he still needs to be announced on the Dodgers’ NLDS roster, which has not been made public yet.
As for Hyeseong Kim, he could be a pinch-runner option if the Dodgers opt to go that route.
More MLB on Heavy: Chicago Cubs Announce Interesting Seiya Suzuki Decision Before MLB Playoffs
What Do Roster Moves Mean for Los Angeles Dodgers Playoff Chances?
If Henriquez can go for the Los Angeles Dodgers’ relief corps, that is a huge boost because he has been one of the team’s breakout pitchers and a highly dependable reliever.
As for the other two moves, they might not be noticeable now, but could play a role down the line.
Ronan Kopp being recalled to the 40-man roster is likely in case of an emergency, but if the Dodgers advance past the NLDS, there’s a slight chance he could be added to the official postseason roster.
Hyeseong Kim is a player who could pay slight dividends on the bases if manager Dave Roberts opts to use him in the late innings as a pinch-runner option.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Edwin Diaz Committed to "Earning" Spot on Postseason Roster
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — Edwin Díaz knows exactly what is at stake over the final days of the regular season. After an injury-plagued year and an uneven return to the majors, the veteran reliever is trying to convince the Dodgers that he belongs in their postseason bullpen. Saturday brought another encouraging step in that direction. Díaz worked a scoreless inning against the Giants and, more importantly, came away feeling that the fastball command that had eluded him earlier in the season is finally b
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Edwin Díaz knows exactly what is at stake over the final days of the regular season.
After an injury-plagued year and an uneven return to the majors, the veteran reliever is trying to convince the Dodgers that he belongs in their postseason bullpen. Saturday brought another encouraging step in that direction.
Díaz worked a scoreless inning against the Giants and, more importantly, came away feeling that the fastball command that had eluded him earlier in the season is finally back.
“Yeah, 100%,” Díaz said when asked if he feels better now than he did before his latest stint in Triple-A. “I’ve been able to throw strikes. I think that was my problem, my concern. I wasn’t throwing my fastball for strikes. Now I’m able to command my fastball really good. And when I command my fastball, my slider plays up.”
That relationship between the two pitches is critical for Díaz. When the fastball is located properly, hitters have a much tougher time distinguishing it from his slider before the breaking ball dives away.
“Right now it’s really good,” Díaz said of the slider. “It’s going down and away. I’ve been able to throw my fastball glove side, so if I throw my fastball glove side, the slider will play off the same path.”
Díaz believes the improvement traces back to a mechanical adjustment made during his time at Oklahoma City.
Following a rough Triple-A appearance, he sat down with the pitching coaches and identified an issue with his hip movement and posture. He said the correction also helped restore an arm slot that had drifted earlier in the season.
“We found I wasn’t moving my hips the right way,” Díaz said. “We started working on that. On Tuesday I threw a really good pen. On Wednesday I pitched, I felt great, and lately I’ve been really good.”
The Dodgers have also been able to ease Díaz back into major league competition without immediately asking him to protect one-run leads in the ninth inning. He said he is perfectly comfortable with that arrangement.
“I’m open-minded right here,” Díaz said. “I need to help this team win. Whatever Doc puts me in the game, in any situation, I will do my job. I feel good. I just want to keep climbing the ladder and finish the season strong.”
That ladder could eventually lead to an October roster spot, but Díaz knows nothing has been guaranteed.
Dave Roberts has acknowledged that there is competition for the final places in a crowded Dodgers bullpen, and Díaz understands that his performance over these final games matters.
“I got to show them that I’m part of that bullpen,” Díaz said. “I haven’t pitched this year, and when I’ve been in the majors, I’ve been struggling. So right now I’m giving my 200% just to show them I will be in that roster spot.”
For Díaz, the path from here is simple: keep throwing strikes, keep getting clean innings, and give the Dodgers a reason to trust him in October.
“Every time they give me the ball, in any situation, I will do my job,” he said. “And then at the end of the season, they will make decisions.”

A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.title: [MLB.com] Pivetta tabbed to start Game 2 after missing most of 2026 with right elbow injury
item.dc:creator: Cole Bradley
item.description: SAN DIEGO -- Through Nick Pivetta’s first four starts this season, it was clear he was picking up right where he left off from his career-best 2025 campaign, one that saw him finish sixth in National League Cy Young Award voting … only for it to be derailed by a right elbow injury in April that cost him nearly five months.
